messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa has been listening with her hands folded over the Book of Shadows at her belt, her attention moving between Vell's face, the empty clerk's desk, and the two strangers she's now bound to. The empty desk pulls at her more than the money does. She was a novice long enough to know the look of a place that has recently lost someone.

When Vell asks if there is anything to ask, she meets his eyes.

"The clerk's room—has anyone else been in it since he died? The landlord, the Watch, his family?" A pause. "And did he die in the faith? I only ask because the dead leave debts of their own, sometimes, and I'd rather not be surprised by one."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell leans an elbow on the counter, eyes drifting once to the empty desk and back to Vell.

"A few things, so we don't waste your daylight." He counts them off on his fingers, the way Vell did.

"What does the box look like: size, wood or iron, and what's the seal? Wax, lead, whose mark? I'd like to know a whole one when I see it."

"Who holds the room now? The cooper, a landlord? Will they let us in on your word, or should we carry a note with your hand on it?"

"How did Jassan die?" He says it plainly, not unkindly. "And has anyone else been asking after his things since? Family, creditors, anyone who isn't you?"

He taps the counter once more. "Last one. If someone's already been in that room before us, do you want to know who, or do you just want the box?"

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I rest my shield against my leg. “Seventy-five gold to carry a box across town. Before we go, Master Vell—how did Ferr die, and is anyone likely to dispute your claim to what’s in his room?”

I glance at the unused desk, then back to him. “We’ll also need a key and a note for his landlord. Something saying we’re collecting on your behalf.”

scenes.narration:
Vell hears all three of them out without interrupting. When Pell starts counting on his fingers, the corner of Vell's mouth moves a little. Then he takes the questions in the order they came.

"The room." He looks at Sefa. "The landlady has been in it. Wenna Pike. She found him. A Fist corporal came and stood there for an hour and wrote something down. Two men from the Song of the Morning carried him out. Then she locked it, as far as I know." He pauses over the second half of her question, longer than over the first. "He gave at the Song of the Morning. Lathander's. What he believed, I never asked. He had a mother once. She's dead. I know of no one else."

He says nothing about the dead leaving debts. He doesn't brush the question aside either. He simply lets it go unanswered.

To Pell: "Oak, bound in iron. About this long." His hands mark something a little longer than a forearm. "Two handles at the ends, a brass plate over the lock. Red wax over the keyhole with my mark pressed into it: a ring with O and V inside. You'll know it." He touches the breast of his waistcoat, where something small and hard sits under the cloth. "The key is here. It stays here. You won't need it."

"He died in his chair. No wound, the corporal said. His heart, I'd guess. He was forty-one and he worked like a man of sixty." For the first time his eyes go toward the empty desk. They stop short of it and come back. "Nobody has asked me for his things. What people ask the landlady, I can't tell you."

He gives Pell's last question more thought than the others. "If someone has been in that room, I want names. Not stories. Names."

To Bram he speaks more shortly, the way one man of business speaks to another. "Nobody can dispute it. The box is mine. The ledgers in it are mine. He took them home to work by his own lamp, which I had told him not to do." He takes a sheet from under the counter, dips a pen and writes four lines in a small, upright hand. He presses his ring into a dab of red wax at the foot of the page and blows on it. "For Mistress Pike. It says you collect on my behalf. I have no key to the room. She has it. The yard belongs to Tobin, the cooper. The rooms above are hers."

He folds the sheet once and leaves it on the counter between the three of them, his ring's mark facing up. Then he picks up a brass weight and sets it carefully on his scale, as if the conversation had already gone out the door. Outside, the hammers have found a common rhythm. The light through the shutters has moved a finger's width along the ledgers.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell slides the folded note off the counter, turns it so the light catches the wax, and studies the mark for a moment: the ring, the O and V, how deep the press sits and how the edge of the ring blurs on one side. He wants to know it by eye when he sees it again on the box.

Then he holds the note out to Bram. "You asked for it, you carry it. Landladies like a man in mail better than a man in leather."

On the way to the door he gives the clerk's desk one last unhurried look: the capped inkwell, the clean blotter, whether a drawer is locked or a scrap of anything is caught under the stool. He doesn't touch it.

At the threshold he nods back to Vell. "Names, not stories. Before nightfall."

Outside, among the hammers, he says quietly to Sefa and Bram, "Coast Way, the cooper's yard. When we get there, let me look at the door and the lock before anyone goes in. If someone's been in that room since the Fist left, it'll show there first."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I take the letter, careful of the wax. “We’ll bring your box back sealed. If it’s already been tampered with, we’ll tell you.”

Outside, I wait for Sefa and Pell before setting off toward the cooper’s yard.

“Let’s speak to Mistress Pike together before we touch anything. She found Ferr; she may have more to tell than his employer.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa waits until Vell has finished speaking to the others, then she reaches for the note, folds it once, and tucks it into her belt beside the Book of Shadows. She meets Vell's eye once more, not with challenge, but with something close to professional care. "We'll see it back to you before nightfall, with the seal as it is." Then, to Pell and Bram, more quietly:

"Let's start with the landlady. Best to hear from her who's been sniffing around before we open the room." A small pause. "And I'd rather see the chair he died in before anyone touches the box."

scenes.narration:
Pell lifts the folded note off the counter and tilts it toward the window. The wax is a deep red, pressed hard and even. Inside the ring the O and the V sit close together, and the V's left stroke runs into the rim. At the bottom of the ring there's a small flat nick where the metal of Vell's ring must be worn. A careful press, and it would be easy to know again. He holds the sheet out to Bram, and Bram takes it by the edges, keeping his thumb off the wax.

Sefa reaches for the note a moment too late. It's already in Bram's hand, so her fingers find only the bare wood of the counter.

*(Out of game: Pell passed the note to Bram first, so Bram has it and Sefa does not.)*

"If it's been tampered with, we'll tell you," Bram says.

"Tell me first." Vell taps the counter once. "Me. Not the corporal, not the landlady." When Sefa promises the seal *as it is*, he gives her a short nod and nothing more.

On his way to the door Pell lets his eye move over the clerk's desk. The inkwell is capped and the blotter is clean. There's one shallow drawer with a small brass keyhole, and it's shut. The tray holds a pen-knife with a worn bone handle, and the floor under the stool has been swept. Nothing is caught there and nothing has been left out. It's the desk of a tidy man, tidied once more by someone else. At the threshold Pell says, "Names, not stories. Before nightfall." Vell is already weighing something, and he doesn't look up.

Outside the hammers are loud. The Coast Way leaves the main street past a farrier's and a chandler's and runs west out of town between low houses and kitchen gardens. The walk takes a quarter of an hour. You smell the cooper's yard before you see it: cut oak, and smoke from a fire where barrel-heads are being charred.

It's an open yard behind a gate of grey planks propped wide. Staves stand in stacks, and iron hoops hang from pegs on the wall like a row of rings. A broad, bald man in a leather apron is driving a hoop down over a cask with a mallet and a set. He doesn't break his rhythm when three armed strangers stop in his gateway, but he does look. That will be Tobin. An outside stair of weathered boards climbs the house wall to a gallery, and two doors open off the gallery. The far one has a padlock through its hasp, new and bright against the old wood.

The near gatepost shows something no one else would read. Down at knee height, where a passer-by's eye never goes, someone has chalked a small circle with a single short tick through its rim. It's a Wide sign from the Gate's roofs, one Pell learned at twelve: *watched — someone's on this house, leave it be.* The chalk is fresh. Nobody has brushed against it yet.

The near door on the gallery opens. A thin woman in a brown shawl comes out with a basket of washing on her hip. She stops at the head of the stair and looks down at the mail, the leather and the shield, holding the basket a little tighter.

screens.Pell Dunmore:
You lift the folded note off the counter and tilt it toward the window. The wax is a deep red, pressed hard and even. Inside the ring the O and V sit close together, and the V's left stroke runs into the rim. At the bottom of the ring there's a small flat nick, where Vell's ring must be worn. It would be easy to know again. You hold the sheet out to Bram, telling him that he asked for it and so he can carry it, since landladies favour a man in mail. Bram takes it by the edges, keeping his thumb off the wax.

Sefa reaches for the note a moment too late; it's already in Bram's hand, and her fingers find only bare counter. Bram says that if the box has been tampered with, they'll tell Vell.

"Tell me first," Vell says, tapping the counter once. "Me. Not the corporal, not the landlady." When Sefa promises the seal will be returned as it is, he gives her a short nod and nothing more.

On your way to the door you let your eye move over the clerk's desk. The inkwell is capped and the blotter is clean. There's one shallow drawer with a small brass keyhole, shut. The tray holds a pen-knife with a worn bone handle, and the floor under the stool has been swept. Nothing is caught there and nothing has been left out. It's the desk of a tidy man, tidied once more by someone else. You touch nothing. At the threshold you tell Vell, "Names, not stories. Before nightfall." He is already weighing something, and he doesn't look up.

Outside, among the hammers, you tell Sefa and Bram quietly that at the cooper's yard on Coast Way you want to look at the door and the lock before anyone goes in, because if someone has been in that room since the Fist left, it will show there first. Bram answers that they should speak to Mistress Pike together before touching anything, since she found Ferr and may know more than his employer. Sefa agrees to start with the landlady, to hear who has been sniffing around, and adds that she'd also like to look at the chair where he died before anyone handles the box.

The Coast Way leaves the main street past a farrier's and a chandler's and runs west out of town between low houses and kitchen gardens. The walk takes a quarter of an hour. You smell the cooper's yard before you see it: cut oak, and smoke from a fire where barrel-heads are being charred.

It's an open yard behind a gate of grey planks propped wide. Staves stand in stacks, and iron hoops hang from pegs on the wall like a row of rings. A broad, bald man in a leather apron is driving a hoop down over a cask with a mallet and a set. He doesn't break his rhythm when three armed strangers stop in his gateway, but he does look. That will be Tobin. An outside stair of weathered boards climbs the house wall to a gallery, and two doors open off it. The far one has a padlock through its hasp, new and bright against the old wood.

The near gatepost shows something no one else would read. Down at knee height, where a passer-by's eye never goes, someone has chalked a small circle with a single short tick through its rim. It's a Wide sign from the Gate's roofs, one you learned at twelve: *watched — someone's on this house, leave it be.* The chalk is fresh. Nobody has brushed against it yet.

The near door on the gallery opens. A thin woman in a brown shawl comes out with a basket of washing on her hip. She stops at the head of the stair and looks down at the mail, the leather and the shield, holding the basket a little tighter.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I keep my sword sheathed and stop clear of Tobin’s work.

“Mistress Pike? Bram Halloway. Master Vell sent us to collect his strongbox from Jassan Ferr’s room. We’ve his letter here.”

I hold up the folded note and wait rather than starting up the stairs.

“Sorry to trouble you after a death in the house. Could you spare us a moment? We’d like to know who’s been in the room, and whether anyone’s come asking after his belongings.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps just inside the gateway, but not too close to the stair, and lifts one empty hand in greeting—keeping the other visibly away from her dagger. She gives the woman with the washing basket a small, open look, the sort she used to give families at the hospice door: steady, unhurried, no threat in it.

"Mistress Pike? Good morning." She nods toward Bram and Pell without turning her head. "We've been sent by Ostrin Vell, about Jassan Ferr's room and the strongbox he kept there. Brought a note for you." A pause. "We're not the Watch, and we're not here to trouble you. But I'd be grateful for a few minutes of your time before we go up."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't stop at the gatepost, and his eyes don't drop to it a second time. He lets Bram go ahead with the note and the mail, and hangs half a step back in the gateway like a man waiting his turn. There he takes in the street the way he used to read a roofline: doorways across the Coast Way, anyone idling in the gardens, a window with a shutter cracked, someone mending something that doesn't need mending. Whoever chalked that wants to see who comes to this door.

He keeps his voice low and easy, meant for Sefa only, not looking at her. "Don't turn round. Someone's marked this house as watched. Old sign, fresh chalk. Somebody's waiting to see who comes for the box. Let's not show we know."

Then, louder and pleasant, as Bram reaches the foot of the stair, Pell lifts his chin toward the gallery and the bright padlock on the far door. "Morning, mistress. Mistress Pike? Master Vell sends us about Jassan's room. That's a handsome new lock. Yours, or did the Fist leave it?"

He gives Tobin a nod in passing as well, friendly, the nod of a man who notices who works where. "And did anyone besides the Fist come asking after him these three days, master cooper? You'd have seen them come through your gate."

<<<
Bram Halloway: I keep my sword sheathed and stop clear of Tobin’s work.

“Mistress Pike? Bram Halloway. Master Vell sent us to collect his strongbox from Jassan Ferr’s room. We’ve his letter here.”

I hold up the folded note and wait rather than starting up the stairs.

“Sorry to trouble you after a death in the house. Could you spare us a moment? We’d like to know who’s been in the room, and whether anyone’s come asking after his belongings.”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa steps just inside the gateway, but not too close to the stair, and lifts one empty hand in greeting—keeping the other visibly away from her dagger. She gives the woman with the washing basket a small, open look, the sort she used to give families at the hospice door: steady, unhurried, no threat in it.

"Mistress Pike? Good morning." She nods toward Bram and Pell without turning her head. "We've been sent by Ostrin Vell, about Jassan Ferr's room and the strongbox he kept there. Brought a note for you." A pause. "We're not the Watch, and we're not here to trouble you. But I'd be grateful for a few minutes of your time before we go up."

Pell Dunmore: Pell doesn't stop at the gatepost, and his eyes don't drop to it a second time. He lets Bram go ahead with the note and the mail, and hangs half a step back in the gateway like a man waiting his turn. Whoever chalked that wants to see who comes to this door.

He keeps his voice low and easy, meant for Sefa only, not looking at her. "Don't turn round. Someone's marked this house as watched. Old sign, fresh chalk. Somebody's waiting to see who comes for the box. Let's not show we know."

Then, louder and pleasant, as Bram reaches the foot of the stair, Pell lifts his chin toward the gallery and the bright padlock on the far door. "Morning, mistress. Mistress Pike? Master Vell sends us about Jassan's room. That's a handsome new lock. Yours, or did the Fist leave it?"

He gives Tobin a nod in passing as well, friendly, the nod of a man who notices who works where. "And did anyone besides the Fist come asking after him these three days, master cooper? You'd have seen them come through your gate."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa’s posture softens a little further at the word debt. She knows unpaid rent; she’s seen what it does to women who keep rooms. She glances once at the new padlock, then back to Wenna.

“The man in the dun coat—did he give you a name, or just coin and curiosity?” She keeps her voice level, as if they were discussing the weather. “And what did he offer, if you don’t mind my asking? A man who comes twice in three days for a dead clerk’s things usually wants more than a coat.”

She lets that sit, then takes a half-step closer to the stair. “You’re owed, and that’s fair. I won’t argue Jassan’s debts are Vell’s to pay. But I’ve silver of my own, and so have my partners here. Let us up to see the room and the box as it was left. If the box is there and the seal whole, your three gold and four silver will be settled before it leaves the room—out of our own purses, not yours, and not Vell’s.” She turns her head enough to include Pell and Bram. “Unless one of you sees it otherwise.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his eyes on the landlady, not the road. On his way forward he passes close behind Sefa and drops four words for her alone: "Crate across the road. Cord."

Then he steps up beside Bram, easy, thumbs in his belt.

"Fair's fair, mistress. A man's debts don't go away because he did." He nods at her shawl where the note went. "How much is left, once the coat's counted? Tell me the sum and I'll settle it here, now, out of my own purse. Master Vell can square it with me after. Then nobody needs to keep thinking about the man in the dun coat." He smiles a little. "And if you'd write a line saying Ferr's rent is paid and by whom, so much the better. Vell likes things in writing."

He lets that sit a moment, then asks the next part lightly, the way you ask about weather.

"This man in the dun coat. Did he give a name? Where he's lodging? What he looked like, young, old, Beregost accent or from away?" A small shrug. "If he means to pay more than a dead clerk's rent for a box of ledgers that aren't his, Master Vell will want to thank him personally."

Last, softer, with a glance up at the gallery: "You said the door wasn't barred when you found him. And the night before Rudd's lock went on, was the room locked at all? Your own key, or just shut?"

He has the coin ready in his hand but doesn't hold it out yet. He waits for her number.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I read the letter, fold it and tuck it into my belt pouch. Then I turn back to Wenna.

“How much is still owing after the coat, Mistress Pike? And did the man in the dun coat give a name—or say why he wanted Ferr’s things?”

I glance toward the road Tobin looked at, keeping my voice level. “We can settle the room before carrying anything out. But I’d want to see that Vell’s box is still there, seal whole, before money changes hands.”

To Sefa and Pell, quietly: “There’s something else we need to discuss in private before we take the box back.”

When he turns his head toward the road the way Tobin's eyes went, he sees the man on the crate under the eaves across the way. The man's chin comes up from his cord at that moment, as it does every few pulls. The two of them look at each other for the space of a breath. Then the man looks down and the cord pulls taut again.

"Two gold and two silver," Wenna says. "The ragman gave me one gold two for the coat. That's what's left. Not a copper more, and I'll not take less." She says it to Pell, because Pell is the one holding the money. Then she looks at Sefa and at Bram. "See it first, then. That's fair. It's there. Nobody's been in."

She answers the rest in the order it came, flat, as if she were reading it off a list.

"No name. He said he came from Master Thale's. Thale lends money on the Trade Way, down past the Jovial Juggler." To Sefa: "More than the rent. That's all you'll have from me on it." To Pell: "Not young, not old. Good boots. Talks like the Gate, quiet. Where he sleeps, he didn't say and I didn't ask."

Then her mouth tightens. "Cooper's got it wrong. Tuesday he didn't come for me. He came for Mister Ferr, knocked on his door, not mine. Mister Ferr wouldn't open to him. I heard him say so through the wood. 'Not today.' Yesterday the man came back, and that time it was me he wanted."

Behind Bram, Tobin's mallet stops for half a stroke and then starts again. He says nothing.

"The door's got its own lock," Wenna goes on, to Pell. "Mister Ferr's key was on his table when I found him. I took it. I've had both keys since Thursday, and I locked it myself when the brothers had gone. Rudd's lock went on the next day, after the man in the dun coat first asked what was left." She pulls her shawl tighter. "A lock's a lock. Two's better when somebody's asking."

To Pell's request for a line in writing, she gives a short dry sound that isn't quite a laugh. "I make my mark. Mister Ferr wrote my rent book for me. You write it and I'll put my mark under."

She turns and climbs back up past the basket of washing. On the gallery she takes a cord from inside her collar with two keys on it, one iron and one bright. The bright one opens Rudd's padlock, and she lifts it out of the hasp. The iron one turns stiffly in the door's own lock. She pushes the door open with two fingers and doesn't go in. She stands to one side of it with the keys in her fist and looks down at the yard.

The room has been shut up for three days, and its air comes out onto the gallery stale. It smells of cold lamp-oil and old paper, with something faintly bitter under it, like a crushed green stalk. From the yard the three of them can see only a slice of it in the daylight: bare boards, the leg of a chair, and the dark edge of a table.

Across the road, the cord has stopped moving.

Characters at the table: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Sefa Marrin: Sefa’s posture softens a little further at the word debt. She knows unpaid rent; she’s seen what it does to women who keep rooms. She glances once at the new padlock, then back to Wenna.

She lets that sit, then takes a half-step closer to the stair. “You’re owed, and that’s fair. I won’t argue Jassan’s debts are Vell’s to pay. But I’ve silver of my own, and so have my partners here. Let us up to see the room and the box as it was left. If the box is there and the seal whole, your three gold and four silver will be settled before it leaves the room—out of our own purses, not yours, and not Vell’s.” She turns her head enough to include Pell and Bram. “Unless one of you sees it otherwise.”

Pell Dunmore: Pell keeps his eyes on the landlady, not the road. On his way forward he passes close behind Sefa and drops four words for her alone: "Crate across the road. Cord."

Then he steps up beside Bram, easy, thumbs in his belt.

Tell me the sum and I'll settle it here, now, out of my own purse. Master Vell can square it with me after. Then nobody needs to keep thinking about the man in the dun coat." He smiles a little. "And if you'd write a line saying Ferr's rent is paid and by whom, so much the better. Vell likes things in writing."

He lets that sit a moment, then asks the next part lightly, the way you ask about weather.

"This man in the dun coat. Did he give a name? Where he's lodging? What he looked like, young, old, Beregost accent or from away?" A small shrug. "If he means to pay more than a dead clerk's rent for a box of ledgers that aren't his, Master Vell will want to thank him personally."

Last, softer, with a glance up at the gallery: "You said the door wasn't barred when you found him. And the night before Rudd's lock went on, was the room locked at all? Your own key, or just shut?"

He has the coin ready in his hand but doesn't hold it out yet. He waits for her number.

Bram Halloway: I read the letter, fold it and tuck it into my belt pouch. Then I turn back to Wenna.

“How much is still owing after the coat, Mistress Pike? And did the man in the dun coat give a name—or say why he wanted Ferr’s things?”

I glance toward the road Tobin looked at, keeping my voice level. “We can settle the room before carrying anything out. But I’d want to see that Vell’s box is still there, seal whole, before money changes hands.”

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell closes his hand on the coin and puts it back in his purse, unhurried. "Two gold, two silver. You'll have it the moment we've seen the box, mistress, and I'll write your line myself."

He goes up the stair lightly, keeping to the wall side where the boards creak least, and stops at the door without crossing the threshold. He takes a breath of that stale air and holds it a moment. Lamp-oil, paper, and that bitter green note under it. A heart that gives out doesn't smell of anything.

He crouches by the lock before anyone goes in, the way he said he would.

He looks at the keyhole of the old iron lock: bright scratches around the mouth or inside, fresh oil or grease where there shouldn't be any, flecks of wax, anything that says a pick or a wrong key has been there. Then the hasp and staple where Rudd's padlock hung: pried, loosened screws, new splinters. Then the frame, the jamb and the sill: tool marks, a scuffed board, dust disturbed in a line along the threshold where a door might have swung on a night it was meant to be shut. Last, the window if there is one off the gallery: the latch, and the sill for dirt or a footprint.

Without looking up, low, to Sefa as she comes up behind him: "Smell that? Bitter. Like a crushed stalk. That's no bad heart." Then, to Bram, just as quiet: "Stay at the head of the stair a moment, would you? Face the yard, not the room. Our friend on the crate has stopped working his cord. I'd like to know if he gets up."

Only when he has finished with the door does he look into the room from the threshold, still not stepping in. He looks for the chair, the table, where the box sits, and whether the dust on the floor between the door and the box has been walked through.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I turn slightly toward Pell and Sefa. “Man under the eaves across the road has been watching us. I’ll keep an eye on him while you look.”

I climb the stairs, leaving room for Pell to examine the doorway first, then take a place on the gallery with a view of the road. I keep my hands away from my weapons.

“Mistress Pike,” I ask quietly, “is that fellow with the cord the man who offered to buy Ferr’s things?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa climbs the stair behind the others and waits on the gallery, not crossing the threshold yet. She doesn't look toward the road, though the corner of her eye is on the shadows.

She takes the string of beads from around her neck, cups them in both palms, and murmurs something low and steady. A soft gold light wakes along the beads, warm as a lamp, and holds. Holding them out toward the dark doorway, she studies what the light finds—the boards, the chair leg, the table edge.

To Wenna, without turning from the door: "Was the shutter as it is now when you found him? And the smell—was the room always so close, or did it smell of something green and bitter even then?" Then, lower, to Pell: "Your eyes before my feet. Tell me where not to step."

scenes.narration:
Pell puts the coin away and goes up the stair close to the wall, where the boards are nailed tightest and give the least. He stops at the door with the toes of his boots short of the sill and crouches by the lock.

It's an old iron box-lock, painted over at some point in the same grey as the door. The mouth of the keyhole is worn smooth, and the scratches around it are all dull: years of a key going in at the same tired angle. There's no grease, no oil, no wax, and no fine bright lines inside the wards of the kind a pick leaves. There is one bright scratch, short, on the lower lip of the keyhole, and he watched it being made two minutes ago when Wenna's key caught and turned stiffly. The hasp's screws are painted in with the door, and the paint over their heads hasn't cracked. Nobody has taken them out. The jamb and the sill have no fresh splinters, no tool bite, no shine where wood has been forced. The room has no window onto the gallery. Its one window is in the far wall, and from the threshold Pell can see the shutter is closed and a wooden bar sits down in its brackets across it.

Bram comes up behind them and takes the corner of the gallery where the stair meets it, with his back to the room and his face to the road. His hands hang empty at his sides. "Mistress Pike. That fellow with the cord. Is he the one who offered for Ferr's things?"

Wenna is still at the far end of the gallery by her own door, and she looks over the yard wall without hiding it. "That's him. Same coat."

Across the road the man in the dun coat stands up as if he has simply finished. He winds the cord around his hand, tucks it into his coat and sets the crate upright against the wall where he found it. He doesn't hurry. He walks up the Coast Way toward the main street and the hammers, an ordinary man going about his day. Where the road bends behind the farrier's hedge he turns his head and looks back once, at the gallery and Bram. Then the hedge hides him.

Sefa takes the beads from her neck and cups them in both hands. She speaks low over them, and the wood wakes: a warm gold glow, steady as a lamp's, spreading out from her palms. She holds it toward the doorway, and the room comes out of the dark.

It's a small room, perhaps twelve feet by ten. A table stands under the barred window. messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“He’s gone toward the main street,” I tell the others quietly. “Wenna confirms he’s Thale’s man. He knows we’re here.”

I stay at the stairhead, watching the approach, and take Odda’s folded letter from my pouch.

“Sefa, Pell—read this when you’ve a moment.” I hold it out toward them. “A plea from Odda Brand. She says her late husband’s debt is in that box, and Vell will take her house once he has it back. She wants the page removed.”

I lower my voice. “I won’t break the seal behind your backs. But before we hand it over, I want to know whether she’s telling the truth—and whether Ferr’s death has anything to do with these debts.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't cross the sill. She holds the glowing beads out before her so the light stays low and level, where it won't stir the dust.

"Pell. The box first, from the doorway. I don't like the wax—it should be Vell's red, not whatever that green-black is. And the floor says no one's walked to it since the place settled."

She reaches out and touches his shoulder with two fingers. A small warmth passes into the leather, like sunlight over skin. "Guidance on your eyes and hands. Stay clear of the bed; the smell is strongest there."

Then to Wenna, without turning: "When you locked up Thursday, was the wax on that box still red? Or was it already dark?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays crouched a moment longer, looking at the floor the way he'd look at a gutter before trusting his weight to it.

"Nobody's been in since Thursday. The dust says so. Let's keep it that way." Without turning, quietly to Sefa: "Bring the light in behind me, close to the box, and step where I step."

He goes in along the right-hand wall, toes into the old softened prints where he can, so as not to lay a fresh trail across the room, and stops by the table. He doesn't touch the box. He gets down on one knee beside it and puts his face close to the seal while Sefa's glow falls on it.

He looks for three things. Is it red under the light, or truly that dark green-black? Is it Vell's mark: the ring with O and V, the V's left stroke running into the rim, the small flat nick at the bottom? And is it whole, with no hairline crack, no lifted edge, no warmed and smoothed look of wax that's been taken off and put back? He checks the brass plate and the hinges too, for pry marks or bright metal.

Then, still on one knee, he reaches for the nightstand with a fold of his sleeve over his fingers, not bare skin. He doesn't pick up the vial, just tilts it toward the light to see if it has a label, a scratched mark, a colour left inside. He takes one cautious sniff from a hand's breadth off and no closer.

Last, the grate. He leans over and looks at the pale curl in the ash without stirring it: paper or parchment, any ink or a corner of writing that survived.

Low, over his shoulder to Sefa: "Tell me if you know that smell. Hospice folk smell more medicine than I do." And, a little louder, toward the door so Bram and Wenna both hear: "Mistress, the bottle by the bed. Was that his, something he took? Or had you never seen it before Thursday?"

screens.Pell Dunmore:
Behind you, Bram speaks low from the corner where the stair meets the gallery, keeping his eye on the Coast Way. He says the man has gone toward the main street, that Wenna confirms he is Thale's man, and that the man knows they are here. He holds out a letter and tells you and Sefa to read it when you can. It is a plea from Odda Brand: her late husband's debt to Vell is in the box, and once Vell has it back he will take her house. She wants the page removed. Bram says he will not break the seal without telling you both, but before the letter is handed over he wants to know if she is honest, and whether Ferr's death is tied to these debts. He stays where he is and does not come toward the room. At the far end of the gallery Wenna watches Sefa's light, not Bram, and her face shows nothing.

Sefa keeps her toes behind the sill and the glowing beads low and level. She says the box should be examined first, from where you are, and that the wax troubles her: it should be Vell's red. She says the floor shows that nobody has crossed to it since the house settled. She touches your shoulder with two fingers and speaks a word under her breath. A small warmth goes into the leather and settles in you, like a hand steadied before fine work. She tells you to stay clear of the bed, where the smell is strongest. Then she asks Wenna, without turning, whether the wax on the box was red or already dark when she locked up on Thursday.

Wenna answers flatly that she never looked at his box. It was under the table then and it is under the table now. She went to him and came out. Red or black, she couldn't say; she wasn't looking at wax.

You go in along the right-hand wall, setting your boots in the old grey prints wherever they fall close enough. The dust takes you lightly, and you still leave one new line of marks that anyone could follow. At the table you go down on one knee beside the box with the gold light at your back.

From a hand's breadth away the seal is nothing like Vell's. It isn't red, and the light doesn't make it red. It is deep bottle-green wax, nearly black where it's thick. Under it, pushed into the mouth of the keyhole, is a soft disc of grey lead. One stamp bit through both wax and lead in a single press. There is no ring and no O or V. It shows a pair of balance-scales with the pans level, and below them an eye drawn closed, a single curved line with short lashes. When the glow lies flat across it, the wax has a faint grain inside it, fine whorled lines under the surface. It looks like a fingerprint until you try to follow the lines and find they don't run the way a fingerprint's do. The edge of the seal is unbroken all the way round: no hairline crack, no lifted lip, none of the glassy, smoothed look of wax that's been warmed and pressed back. The brass plate and iron hinges are dull and even, with no bright metal and no bite of a tool. Three days of dust lie as thin on the lid as on the floor.

With your sleeve over your fingers you tilt the vial on the nightstand toward the light. It has no label and no paper tied round its neck. Near the base someone has scratched a little sunburst into the glass, a circle with short rays, done quickly with a point. A dark greenish-brown film has dried inside. From a hand's breadth away the smell is a crushed green bitterness, and under it the sharp ghost of spirits, the way a tincture made in alcohol smells.

You asked Wenna about the bottle, and she answers from the gallery: it was his. He kept it by the bed and took it with his water at night. Where he had it from, he didn't say. She pauses and adds that she didn't ask him that either.

Last, you lean over the cold grate to look at the pale curl in the ash without stirring it.

- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her toes behind the sill and the light steady, though her voice is low and firm enough to carry only to Pell.

"Come back over, Pell. The seal's not cut, but it's not Vell's either. Green wax set over lead, pressed with scales and a closed eye." She doesn't look at the box again while she says it. "Leave it as it lies. I won't have us break the dust around it until we've decided, all three, what to carry back and what to say when we do."

Then she tips her head slightly toward Bram, still at the stairhead. "Fold it, Bram. Not here. We'll read it away from the yard and away from the road." To Wenna she says, just loud enough, "Mistress Pike—on the nights you took up his supper, did he drink from that little glass before you? Every night? And did he ever say who it was prepared by, whether a temple sold it to him?"

She reaches out with her free hand to steady Pell's arm as he crosses back over the threshold, then lifts her beads and lets the glow catch the doorway once more, taking in the chair and the table's shadow from outside, not from within. After a silence she adds, more to herself than anyone:

"Scales with an eye closed. That may just be a lending-house's mark—or something older. If either of you knows it, say so now."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays bent over the grate a breath longer and says the line over twice under his breath, until he has it by heart: *To Sergeant Cowl of the Fist… the notes were sold before the wagons.* He doesn't touch the paper. It would go to powder at a finger, and it's worth more lying where Jassan left it than in Pell's pocket.

He backs out the way he came, boots in his own prints, and stops beside Sefa at the sill. He speaks low, for her and for Bram at the stairhead, not for Wenna.

"Three things. The box is Vell's: oak, iron, brass, the size he showed us. Nobody's touched it since Thursday. But the seal isn't his. Green wax over lead, one press through both. Balance-scales, pans level, and an eye shut under them. Unbroken. Someone sealed that box before Jassan died, and it wasn't Vell." He tips his head at the nightstand. "The bottle was his medicine, Wenna says. Somebody scratched a sunburst on the glass. That's Lathander's mark, or someone wanting it to look like Lathander's. And in the grate, a letter he started to Sergeant Cowl of the Fist and then burned: *the notes were sold before the wagons.* Wagons. Caravans go missing on the Way south of here."

He holds out his hand to Bram for the letter. "Let me see Odda's page." He reads it quickly at the stairhead, then hands it back.

"Here's where I stand. We don't break that seal. Not for Odda, not for anyone. Once it's broken, we're thieves and Vell's liars both. We carry it to him as it is, and before he so much as touches it we tell him the wax is wrong, so he hears it from us first, the way he asked. Then we watch his face when he sees that eye. That'll tell us more than the ledgers would." A glance up the empty road. "And Thale's man knows we're here. We walk it back together, by the main street, in daylight."

Then, louder, he turns to Wenna with the coin already counted into his palm: two gold, two silver.

"Your sum, mistress. Ferr's paid." He tips it into her hand. "Have you a scrap of paper and a stub of charcoal? I'll write that you had it from Pell Dunmore on Vell's behalf, and you put your mark under." While she looks, more gently: "Before Thursday, did anyone else climb that stair to him? Not the dun coat. Anyone from the Song, a brother bringing his medicine? Or someone carrying wax and a seal?"

He adds one more thing before anyone lifts the box. "Leave the bottle and the grate exactly as they lie, and lock it up with both locks once we're gone. If a Fist sergeant named Cowl ever comes asking, he'll want to see that room as it is."

Last, to Bram: "You've the arms for it. I'll take the stair ahead of you." He goes back in along his own line of prints, ready to steady the near handle once Bram lifts the box from under the table.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I tuck Odda’s letter away for now and keep watch over the yard and road.

“Mistress Pike—did Ferr have any visitors besides Thale’s man in his last few days? Anyone bringing his medicine?”

Then, quietly toward the room: “Pell, what have you found? If that seal’s been altered, we should all see it before the box moves.”

cards.title: Religion: do the scales over a closed eye belong to some temple's old mark?

presses.text:
You keep the beads lifted as Pell steps over the sill, and for a moment the gold light passes over your own hands and his, making them both look warm and steady. At the far end of the gallery Wenna takes the coins from Pell and closes her fingers over them, then listens to his questions with her chin down, the two keys still in her other fist.

She answers you first, when there is a quiet moment: she only saw the little glass from the doorway when she brought him his water and his supper, and she didn't study whether he drank it before her or after. She didn't ask where he had it from, and he didn't offer. She only knew it was his medicine by the way he spoke of it—"my night dose," he called it.

To Pell she says no one from the Song came before Thursday. The brothers only came Thursday, two of them, with their board and a sheet to carry him on. As for the seal and the wax, she says she saw no wax and no seal, and doesn't know what he's asking. But she nods at the rest: the room will stay locked with both locks, the bottle and grate as they are. If this Corporal Cowl or any Fist man asks, she'll say she kept it shut. She and Pell write his line on a smooth bit of board-paper with a charcoal from the yard, and she makes her mark under it, a firm X pressed with her thumb.

Then it is your turn, and you look at the green wax still lying under the table. The smooth disc of lead catching the lamplight-gold, the two scales balanced, and the single long closed eye beneath them, lashes drawn like a woman asleep or a corpse laid out. You turn the mark over in your mind against every temple seal you learned at the hospice, every patron's symbol the sisters taught you to know for the dying, and every old sign you've seen scrawled on remedies or charms in the Lower City.

What comes to you is this, in a slow, unwelcome way:

You know the balance scales as a mark of Waukeen, goddess of trade, coin and honest weight. Lathander's sunburst you'd know anywhere; the glass by the bed carries a rough but true likeness of it, and no temple you've met would sell an unlabelled vial for three days after death. But the closed eye? It is not Waukeen's, and not Tyr's blindfold. The line of lashes drawn downward—it stirs an older memory, half-text and half-warning: among the long-dead remnants of the Bhaal-cult, written in blood and old ink, the eye of murder was an open spiral. A closed eye belongs to no god of the Gate that you can name. It reads like one sign laid above another, or a private seal made to look half sacred. And the scales above it lie level, which is the worst part, because level scales mean a debt already weighed and paid.

The crumbs and threads of your knowing come to rest there. You are certain enough of what it is not; of what it is, you have only a conviction like cold water down the back.

[Roll card] Sefa Marrin · Skill check — Religion: +4 vs DC 15. The die is cast on the server; tap it to see how it fell.
presses.reply:
Thanks, that's a vivid picture of Sefa at work, and I'll use it. Here is how I'll take it when the die lands.

Sefa's part is hers and stands as written. She keeps the beads raised for Pell, looks at the green seal under the table, and searches her memory against every temple mark, deathbed sign and Lower City charm she has known. That's exactly what the Religion card is testing, so the card stays.

What she actually remembers is decided by the die, and the content comes from the world, not from the proposal. A few honest flags so nothing surprises you:

- In the Realms as I'm running them, level scales are most familiar as Tyr's sign (scales balanced on a warhammer). Waukeen's is a gold coin with a woman's face. Sefa's hospice learning points that way first, not toward Waukeen.
- The open-spiral "eye of murder" and "level scales mean a debt already paid" aren't established facts of this world. Whatever the closed eye is, Sefa learns as much as the roll earns her and no more.
- Pell and Wenna's exchange belongs to Pell's player and to me. Pell said he'd pay once the box has been seen. He hasn't handed the coin over yet, Wenna hasn't made her mark, and her answers to Pell are mine to give when he asks. I won't play them from Sefa's card.
- One small mix-up: Cowl is the *Sergeant* named on the burnt draft in the grate. The man who came Thursday was an unnamed Fist *corporal* with a squint. As far as anyone here knows, they aren't the same man.

Wenna did say the little glass was his, kept by the bed and taken with his water at night. Anything more she knows or doesn't, she'll tell Sefa herself if Sefa asks her next round.

Roll when you're ready. I'll narrate what Sefa makes of the seal from how the die falls.

presses.text:
I rock back a little on my heels, the beads steady in my hand but my eyes shut a moment longer than a blink. I think of the gate-keeper at the hospice, her finger on the row of seals, naming each for the fear that came with it: Tymora for the gambler, Helm for the soldier, Waukeen for the merchant, Bhaal for no one.

And I see it, in the dust where the seal lies under the table: two scales level, the eye closed, lashes drawn down. Not Waukeen. Not Tyr's blindfold. An accounting made and paid, with the eye that need not see. It could be a private mark; the Road is thick with moneylenders' badges. But a private mark on a dead clerk's strongbox, set over lead and green wax, a day or a night before his heart gave out—that is not private. That is a message. And if anything of Bhaal's old hand is under that eye-lid, then someone in Beregost has put their thumb in something older than Vell's ledgers.

Which means the name I am not going to say in this doorway is: this was not a debt. It was a reckoning.

So I keep it. I let the light fall along the floor, toward the box without touching it, and say to Pell and Bram, low, as if explaining the shape of the ceiling:

"The scales are Waukeen's, the same scales you'd see over a counting-house. But the eye under them isn't hers, and it isn't Tyr's. I've seen it once before, in an old grave-mark, in the crypt of a Lower City house: a closed eye over a level scale, like a debt weighed and paid. If it is what I think, then Jassan didn't just die with his box. He was marked before he died."

I lift the beads and turn so the light reveals my face, and mine only. "Whatever we do, don't scrape that wax, and don't breathe a word of it until we're clear of the yard."

presses.text:
Sefa’s eyes narrow at the green wax as the fragments fall into place at last. She lowers the beads a fraction, and the light runs along the fine whorls in the glassy surface.

“I know it,” she says quietly. "From the hospice. I saw the description in an ancient book—kept behind the altar cloth, read once by the gate-keeper, then taken to be burned. The scales level, with an eye closed under them. It is the sign of Bhaal."

She turns to the others, her face lit from below by the glow of the beads. "It marks a price paid. They seal a balance with it—an account settled. Jassan's death was not chance." Her voice is low, but certain. "The mark is not a debt; it is a receipt."

She lifts her hand from Pell's arm and points, not with a finger but with the edge of the light, toward the wax. "Look—close, but do not touch: the eye is not drawn as through sleep; the lashes are drawn downward, like a lid closed by another hand. That is the old sign. And the scales are level. It is finished." She breathes out, as if naming it in the open air costs her something. "We carry the box, but we should not pretend it is only Vell's. It has been sealed, after its owner, by someone who serves the god of murder."

You hold the light a little higher, and the whorled wax seems to drink it and give nothing back. The design is steady now, no longer wavering at the edge of your memory: level scales, a line of lashes drawn downward, an eye gone still as a stone in a pan. It is the sign of Bhaal—not the public mark of the old temple, but the private cipher of a cultist's accounting, pressed into wax over lead like a ledger's final line. A death already weighed, already closed, already receipted.

The sisters once made you learn the old signs so you would know when a dying man had already been claimed before you touched him. The gate-keeper had shown you the page and then fed it to the brazier, making you both watch.

Now here it is again, three days old and lying quietly under a moneylender's table in Beregost.

You say it aloud, low, to Pell and Bram. Pell goes entirely still; Bram's head comes round a few degrees from the road. Wenna, too far down the gallery to make out more than the shape of the words, only sees the three of you draw together and the light dip.

The strongbox has not moved. It sits where Ferr left it, or where the one who sealed it left it, the closed white eye glinting faintly beneath the scales. It is very quiet in the room again. Below, in the yard, the far door creaks as Tobin rolls a fresh cask across the flags.

Where you are: on the gallery outside Ferr's room, gold light in hand · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 8 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

opening.narration:
Beregost wakes to hammers. From every smithy along the street the ringing comes through the shutters of Ostrin Vell's counting-house, where the morning light falls on brass scales and rows of bound ledgers. Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway stand at the long counter. The three of you met here only this morning, and Vell has just hired you together.

Vell lays the terms out a second time, tapping the counter with one finger at each point. Jassan Ferr, his clerk, died three days ago in a rented room above the cooper's yard on the Coast Way. In that room is a locked strongbox of ledgers. Vell wants it here before nightfall today, unopened, with its seal whole. On delivery he will pay seventy-five gold for the three of you to share. Not a copper before.

Beside the counter stands a clerk's desk. Its stool is pushed neatly under it, the inkwell is capped and the blotter is clean, as if someone had tidied it and no one had sat there since. Vell does not look at it. He looks from Sefa to Pell to Bram, folds his hands on the counter and waits. "The Coast Way is not far, and the day will not wait for you. Is there anything you need to ask me before you go?"
